meta.titre: Modular Arithmetic: Remainders, power cycles and unit digits

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Further Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Every evening a trader in Limbe counts her unsold mangoes and packs them into crates of the same size: what matters is how many are left over, not how many there are. Remainders also decide which weekday a date falls on, how the check digit of a barcode is computed. Modular arithmetic is the algebra of remainders. In the Cameroon GCE Further Mathematics Paper 1 it gives short, high-value questions on unit digits and remainders of huge powers that are impossible by direct calculation but easy with congruences.

items: Division with remainder: any integer $a$ can be written $a=nq+r$ with $n>0$ and $0\le r<n$.
An integer $d$ divides $m$ when $m=dk$ for some integer $k$.
The unit digit of a positive integer is its remainder on division by $10$.

sections.titre: Congruences, power cycles and Fermat's little theorem
sections.contenu_markdown:
Two integers $a$ and $b$ are **congruent modulo $n$**, written $a\equiv b\pmod n$, when $n$ divides $a-b$. Equivalently, they leave the same remainder on division by $n$. The remainder of $a$ on division by $n$ is the unique $r$ with $0\le r<n$ and $a\equiv r\pmod n$. For a negative number the remainder is still non-negative: since $-17=5\times(-4)+3$, the remainder of $-17$ on division by $5$ is $3$.

If $a\equiv b$ and $c\equiv d\pmod n$ then

$$
a+c\equiv b+d,\qquad a-c\equiv b-d,\qquad ac\equiv bd,\qquad a^{k}\equiv b^{k}\pmod n\tag{1}
$$

so you may replace any number by a smaller one with the same remainder before calculating. Division is not allowed in general.

**Power cycles.** The remainders of $a^{1},a^{2},a^{3},\dots$ modulo $n$ repeat. Suppose the cycle (starting from $a^{1}$) has length $p$. Write the exponent as $k=pq+j$ with $1\le j\le p$; then

$$
a^{k}\equiv a^{j}\pmod n\tag{2}
$$

so you reduce the **exponent modulo the cycle length**, and an exponent that is a multiple of $p$ gives the **last** member of the cycle ($j=p$). For example, modulo $10$ we have $7^{4}\equiv1$ and $2^{4}\equiv6$. For unit digits (modulo $10$):

| Last digit of base | Cycle of last digits | Length |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1, 5, 6 | constant (0, 1, 5, 6) | 1 |
| 4 | 4, 6 | 2 |
| 9 | 9, 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 2, 4, 8, 6 | 4 |
| 3 | 3, 9, 7, 1 | 4 |
| 7 | 7, 9, 3, 1 | 4 |
| 8 | 8, 4, 2, 6 | 4 |

To find the unit digit of a sum, find the unit digit of each term and add them, reducing modulo $10$ at the end.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the modulus is a prime $p$ and the base is not a multiple of $p$.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
If $p$ is prime and $p\nmid a$ then
$$
a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\tag{3}
$$
so exponents can be reduced modulo $p-1$. For example, modulo $7$ the exponent of $a$ can be reduced modulo $6$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must solve for $x$ in a congruence.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If $\gcd(a,n)=1$ there is an inverse $a'$ with $aa'\equiv1\pmod n$ (found by trial or by Euclid's algorithm). Multiply both sides by $a'$ to get $x\equiv a'b\pmod n$, a single solution modulo $n$. If $ka\equiv kb\pmod n$ and $g=\gcd(k,n)$, you may cancel $k$ only if you also divide the modulus: $a\equiv b\pmod{n/g}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the base is just below a multiple of the modulus.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If the base is $\equiv-1\pmod n$ then $a^{k}\equiv(-1)^{k}$, which is $1$ for even $k$ and $-1\equiv n-1$ for odd $k$. For example $6\equiv-1\pmod7$, so $6^{85}\equiv-1\equiv6\pmod7$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student finds the remainder of $-17$ on division by $5$ as $-2$ because $-17=5\times(-3)-2$.
items.pourquoi_faux: A remainder must satisfy $0\le r<n$. The value $-2$ is congruent to the correct remainder but is not itself the remainder.

items.erreur_markdown: To find $3^{100}$ modulo $7$ a student writes $3^{100}\equiv3^{100\bmod7}=3^{2}=9\equiv2$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The exponent must be reduced modulo the length of the cycle of powers, not modulo $7$. The powers of $3$ modulo $7$ are $3,2,6,4,5,1$, a cycle of length $6$ (Fermat: $3^{6}\equiv1$).

items.erreur_markdown: A student sees $6\times4\equiv6\times1\pmod9$ and cancels the $6$ to conclude $4\equiv1\pmod9$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Cancellation is allowed only when the factor has no common divisor with the modulus. Here $\gcd(6,9)=3$, so the modulus must be divided by $3$.
items.correction_markdown: $4\equiv1\pmod3$, which is true. Modulo $9$ the statement $4\equiv1$ is false.

items.erreur_markdown: A student says the unit digit of $7^{2024}$ is $7$, because "$2024$ is a multiple of $4$, so we start the cycle again".
items.pourquoi_faux: When the exponent is a multiple of the cycle length $4$, the power is $\left(7^{4}\right)^{506}\equiv1$, the last member of the cycle, not the first.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Find the remainder when $-59$ is divided by $8$.

(b) Find the remainder when $345\times678$ is divided by $11$, without multiplying the two numbers.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $-59=8\times(-8)+5$, so the remainder is **$5$**.

(b) $345=11\times31+4$, so $345\equiv4$, and $678=11\times61+7$, so $678\equiv7\pmod{11}$. Therefore $345\times678\equiv4\times7=28\equiv$ **$6$** $\pmod{11}$.

Work modulo $10$.

$14\equiv4$ and the powers of $4$ alternate $4,6$; the exponent $2027$ is odd, so $14^{2027}\equiv4$.

The powers of $9$ alternate $9,1$; the exponent is odd, so $9^{2027}\equiv9$.

The powers of $8$ cycle $8,4,2,6$. Since $2027=4\times506+3$, $8^{2027}\equiv8^{3}\equiv2$.

Sum $\equiv4+9+2=15\equiv5$. The unit digit is **$5$**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Solve the congruence $7x\equiv4\pmod{11}$, giving the solution with $0\le x<11$.

(b) Use Fermat's little theorem to find the remainder when $6^{100}$ is divided by $13$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $7\times8=56=5\times11+1$, so $8$ is the inverse of $7$ modulo $11$. Multiplying by $8$: $x\equiv8\times4=32\equiv$ **$10$** $\pmod{11}$. Check: $7\times10=70=6\times11+4$.

(b) $13$ is prime and does not divide $6$, so $6^{12}\equiv1\pmod{13}$. Since $100=12\times8+4$, $6^{100}\equiv6^{4}=1296$. Now $1296=13\times99+9$, so the remainder is **$9$**.

items_markdown: $a\equiv b\pmod n$ means $n\mid(a-b)$, i.e. the same remainder; remainders are always in $0,1,\dots,n-1$, even for negative numbers.
Congruences can be added, subtracted, multiplied and raised to powers, so replace big numbers by small congruent ones.
For powers, find the cycle of remainders and reduce the exponent modulo the cycle length; a multiple of the length gives the last member of the cycle.
Unit digit means modulus $10$; for a sum, find each unit digit and add them.
Fermat: $a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p$ for prime $p$ not dividing $a$. Cancel a common factor only after dividing the modulus by its gcd with that factor.
